topics.title: Film form in US cinema, Silent Era to 1990

outcomes.text: Study one US set film from each period: Silent Era, 1930-1960 and 1961-1990.
Explain how micro-elements of film form construct meaning and contribute to film aesthetics.
Explain film poetics: a film as a constructed artefact formed by selection and combination.
Analyse camera shots, depth of field, angles, hand-held versus steadicam, composition and monochrome cinematography.
Explain three-point lighting, chiaroscuro and other expressive lighting and how they convey character and atmosphere.
Explain how cinematography generates multiple connotations, psychological insight and different spectator readings.
Analyse setting, props, costume and make-up and how they build character, narrative, messages and values.
Explain naturalistic versus expressive mise-en-scene, motifs, staging, movement and off-screen space.
Explain continuity editing, match editing, the 180 degree rule and the Kuleshov effect.
Analyse montage and stylised editing such as jump cuts, editing motifs and post-production visual effects.
Distinguish parallel from contrapuntal sound, diegetic from non-diegetic sound, foley and expressive sound.
Explain sound motifs, multitrack mixing, layering, asynchronous sound and sound design.
Analyse non-verbal communication, performance styles (method, improvisatory), casting and actor interaction.
Explain directing as choreography and how performance relates to cinematography.
Explain how each micro-element can indicate an auteur approach and why spectators read the same element differently.
Explain how mise-en-scene, cinematography, composition, framing, music and editing create aesthetic effects.
Discuss the conflict between spectacle and narrative resolution.
Relate film aesthetics to auteurism and ideology.
Explain plot, temporal duration and ellipsis in narrative construction.
Analyse narrational devices: voiceover, flashback, framing narrative, open ending and patterning.
Explain how dramatic qualities and dialogue construct a scene and give psychological insight into character.
Analyse narratives that reject the three-act structure, including non-linear narratives.
Study the set pair of European surrealist films and define experimental film as non-narrative or working against narrative conventions.
Explain experimental narrative forms that oppose conventional structures.
Study at least one set film from German expressionism or French new wave.
Explain the contexts and shared stylistic or political aims of the two movements studied.
Apply micro-elements and film aesthetics to the European films studied.
Explain the social, cultural, political, historical and institutional contexts of the films studied.
Debate formalist and structuralist conceptions of film narrative.
Debate the claims of naturalism and realism against the expressive.
Study one contemporary British and one contemporary US set film.
Explain how film form, narrative and genre create representations of societies and cultures.
Debate the significance of the digital in film and new possibilities for cinema.
Explain how viewing conditions affect spectators.
Evaluate auteurism and its continued validity as a theory.
Study one set documentary film in depth, with its micro-elements, conventions and contexts.
Explain how form, narrative and generic conventions represent reality and societies.
Explain modes of documentary filmmaking and claims of naturalism and realism.
Explain the documentary theories of John Grierson and D.A. Pennebaker and apply them to the set film.
Study three set films from one theme (Family and Home, Outsiders or Conflict), one from each of US independent, English-language non-US and non-European non-English-language.
Explain how films shape and are shaped by ideology and compare how messages and values arise from context.
Explain how micro-elements and narrative align the spectator with characters' points of view.
Explain how narrative construction and structure shape ideologies and can act as an ideological framework.
Analyse the ideological implications of representations of different societies and cultures.
Explain genre conventions and genre as a principal structuring element of narrative.
Explain how film form, genre and narrative produce representations of cultures and societies.
Explain the ideological implications of representations in film.
Explain how films reflect and construct social, cultural and political attitudes.
Explain how films reflect historical issues and events and can help drive social change.
Explain intertextual references and how films reflect production, financial and technological constraints.
Compare passive and active conceptions of the spectator and the spectator's interaction with narrative.
Explain uniformity and diversity of response, and the effect of social and cultural factors.
Analyse narrative, visual, musical, performance, genre and auteur cues in relation to response.
Explain preferred, negotiated, oppositional and aberrant readings and the impact of viewing conditions.
Explain visual effects, their intended emotional response and the spectator's actual response.
Discuss the relevance of auteurism to collaborative filmmaking.
